cues.text: Kit puts the two articles side by side, and notices they are arguing about the same quantity from opposite sides.
One of them asserts that a lower cost of capital raises investment.
And the other spends a whole article showing that the number standing between the cost of capital and the decision is not the cost of capital.
The bar a project must clear is the textbook bar, multiplied.
And the multiplier grows as the world becomes more uncertain.
Which means we can go back to the sheet from chapter eight, and watch what the policy actually does to a firm's bar.
Here is a firm in ordinary times. Twenty per cent choppiness, money at five per cent. Its bar is one point eight six times break-even.
The policy makes money cheaper. So the firm slides this way — and the sheet under it goes up, not down. Two point six one.
But the policy is only ever used in a crisis. So at the very same moment, the firm is dragged the other way too — into the choppiest part of the sheet.
Both movements push the bar up. Not one up and one down. Both up.
Which gives the sentence this chapter exists for. Quantitative easing is not a weaker version of a rate cut. It is a rate cut delivered in the one situation that blunts rate cuts.
And be clear about whose is whose. The bar, and the fact that it rises with uncertainty, is Dixit's.
Putting it next to this policy is Kit's.

cheaper money moves the firm up the sheet
and a crisis moves it up the other way too
a rate cut delivered where rate cuts are blunted
